Simulate Power Analysis for Lineup Studies

Source: R/simulate_lineup_data.R
simulate_power_analysis.Rd

Estimates statistical power to detect a difference in discriminability between two lineup conditions, by simulating both conditions at a range of sample sizes and recording how often the difference is detected.

Usage

simulate_power_analysis(
  sample_sizes,
  d_prime,
  d_prime_null = 0,
  n_simulations = 1000,
  test_function = NULL,
  alpha = 0.05,
  lineup_size = 6,
  n_bootstrap = 200,
  seed = NULL,
  verbose = TRUE,
  ...
)

Arguments

sample_sizes

Integer vector. Sample sizes per condition to test (e.g., c(50, 100, 200)). Each is used for both target-present and target-absent lineups in each condition.

d_prime

Numeric. Discriminability of the condition of interest.

d_prime_null

Numeric. Discriminability of the comparison condition. Defaults to 0, which asks how often the procedure can be shown to discriminate better than chance. Set it to a non-zero value to ask the more usual question of how often two working procedures can be told apart.

n_simulations

Integer. Number of simulated studies per sample size (default = 1000). Power is a proportion estimated from these, so its own standard error is roughly sqrt(0.25 / n_simulations).

test_function

Function of two dataframes returning a p-value. Defaults to a bootstrap comparison of partial AUC via compare_pauc.

alpha

Numeric. Significance level (default = 0.05)

lineup_size

Integer. Lineup size for both conditions (default = 6)

n_bootstrap

Integer. Bootstrap resamples used by the default test (default = 200). This is the dominant cost: the default test is run n_simulations times for every sample size.

seed

Optional integer seed for reproducibility.

verbose

Logical. Report progress (default = TRUE).

...

Additional arguments passed to simulate_lineup_data(), for example conf_levels or foil_bias.

Value

A dataframe of class power_analysis with columns:

  • sample_size: N per condition

  • power: Proportion of simulated studies reaching significance

  • power_se: Standard error of that proportion

  • mean_effect: Mean observed difference in pAUC

  • sd_effect: Standard deviation of the observed difference

  • n_valid: Simulations that produced a usable test

Details

Power is the probability that a study of a given size detects an effect that is really there. Estimating it by simulation means specifying the effect, generating many studies of that size, applying the analysis you intend to use, and counting how often it reaches significance.

That requires a null to test against, which is what d_prime_null supplies. Simulating a single condition and computing a statistic from it is not a power analysis, because no hypothesis is being tested.

See also

compare_pauc, simulate_lineup_data

Examples

# \donttest{
# Power to show discriminability better than chance
power_res <- simulate_power_analysis(
  sample_sizes = c(50, 100),
  d_prime = 1.5,
  n_simulations = 8,
  n_bootstrap = 50,
  conf_levels = 5,
  seed = 123
)
#> Simulating sample size 50 (8 studies)
#> Simulating sample size 100 (8 studies)
print(power_res)
#>   sample_size power  power_se mean_effect  sd_effect n_valid
#> 1          50 0.875 0.1169268  0.04444208 0.01567793       8
#> 2         100 1.000 0.0000000  0.04280260 0.01922859       8
# }
